founded.what: The year the business was established at Reims by the father-in-law of Barbe-Nicole Ponsardin, the widow who took it over in 1805, by the house.

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: it grows much of its Pinot Noir in Grand Cru villages, buys more from growers in fifty or sixty crus and makes the wine itself.

story: Veuve Clicquot was established at Reims in 1772, by the house's account, by the father of the man Barbe-Nicole Ponsardin married. In 1805, widowed at twenty seven, Barbe-Nicole Clicquot Ponsardin (1777 to 1866) took over the business, and the house took its name from her title, the widow Clicquot. The house credits her with the riddling table in 1816, the ancestor of the rack, made to clear the wine of its sediment, and with the first known blended rosé Champagne in 1818, made by adding red wine to white. She chose her partner as her successor: he officially became head of the company in 1841, and she died in 1866. Louis Vuitton bought the house in 1986, and it joined the Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton group in 1987. La Grande Dame, named for the widow, was first made in the 1962 vintage and launched in 1972 for the house's bicentenary. From the 2008 vintage, by the house, its share of Pinot Noir rose to about nine tenths, with Chardonnay for the rest.

style.line: Pinot Noir leads, full and toasty, with a broad, generous finish: a deep stock of reserve wines and Grand Cru Pinot Noir of the Montagne de Reims give the house its weight.
style.grapes: Pinot Noir leads, with Chardonnay and Meunier, from fifty to sixty crus; Yellow Label is about half Pinot Noir, near a third Chardonnay and a sixth or so Meunier, by the house.
style.reserve: Blends hold up to half reserve wines, by the house, from some 400 reserve wines of 17 years; Yellow Label holds 30 to 45 per cent by its pages.
style.vessels: Stainless steel vats above all, with a small share fermented and aged in large oak casks for the vintage wines, by the house.
style.malolactic: Generally carried out, by the house, but stopped in some of its wineries since 2018 to keep the blends fresh after warmer harvests.
style.lees: At least 30 months for the non vintage wines by one of the house's pages, and three years for Yellow Label by another.
style.dosage: 9 to 10 grams a litre for Yellow Label by the house's pages and the trade, and 6 for La Grande Dame 2015, by the house.

nv.name: Yellow Label
nv.note: The non vintage Brut a guest knows by its colour before reading the label: about half Pinot Noir, with Chardonnay and Meunier, and a large share of reserve wines.

cuvee.name: La Grande Dame

first.what: The first vintage, launched in 1972 for the house's bicentenary; accounts differ on whether a later vintage was the first sold widely.

cuvee.rhythm: Made only in years the house declares since the 1962: the 1990, 2004, 2006, 2008, 2012 and 2015 are among them, the 1990 also in magnum and jeroboam.
cuvee.blend: Pinot Noir leads, about nine parts in ten since the 2008 by the house, with Chardonnay for the rest; earlier vintages held between half and two thirds Pinot Noir.
cuvee.sites: The house's eight historical Grand Cru villages: Pinot Noir from Aÿ, in the Vallée de la Marne, and Verzenay, Verzy, Ambonnay and Bouzy, on the Montagne de Reims; Chardonnay from Avize, Oger and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, on the Côte des Blancs.
cuvee.making: The base wines ferment chiefly in stainless steel, with a small share in large oak casks for the house's vintage wines. Pinot Noir from the cooler, later ripening north facing slopes of the Montagne de Reims gives the wine its spine, by Decanter. The 2015 was dosed at 6 grams a litre, by the house.
cuvee.lees: The house gives no figure on the pages read; reviews date disgorgings of the 2015 to October 2021 and July 2023, six to eight years after the harvest.
cuvee.young: Jasmine and acacia opening onto pear and clementine, by the house's own note, with oyster shell and green apple at first and honey, nutmeg and a touch of ginger as it breathes.
cuvee.aged: With age it turns to gunflint, coffee and crusty bread, then hazelnut, cashew, beeswax and honey, by the house's note on its 1990.

forms.name: La Grande Dame Rosé
forms.note: The same vintage wine coloured with red Pinot Noir from the house's Clos Colin vineyard, about an eighth of the blend in the 2015, by the house.

cuvee.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass.

table.house45: Veuve Clicquot is the house of Reims that carries a widow's title. Barbe-Nicole Clicquot took it over in 1805, at twenty seven, and ran it for decades. The house credits her with the riddling table, which clears the wine of its sediment, and with the first known blended rosé, in 1818. The style is led by Pinot Noir, full and toasty, built on a deep store of reserve wines. Yellow Label is the bottle guests know by its colour. The prestige cuvée is La Grande Dame, named for her and first made in 1962.
table.house10: Veuve Clicquot is the Reims house of the widow Clicquot, Pinot Noir led and toasty, famous for its Yellow Label.
table.cuvee45: La Grande Dame is the prestige Champagne of Veuve Clicquot, named for the widow who made the house. It was first made in 1962 and launched in 1972 for the house's two hundredth year. It comes from eight Grand Cru villages, and since 2008 it has been about nine parts Pinot Noir to one of Chardonnay. That Pinot Noir grows on the cool slopes of the Montagne de Reims, which keeps it fresh. Expect jasmine, pear and clementine, with a touch of honey and ginger. I serve it cool rather than cold, in a white wine glass.
table.sale: If you want a Champagne with a woman's story behind it, La Grande Dame is Veuve Clicquot's tribute to the widow, nearly all Grand Cru Pinot Noir. May I bring a bottle for the table?
table.cuvee10: La Grande Dame is Veuve Clicquot's vintage prestige cuvée, Grand Cru Pinot Noir led, named for the widow Clicquot.
table.cuvee20: La Grande Dame is the vintage prestige cuvée of Veuve Clicquot, first made in 1962 and named for the widow. It is about nine parts Grand Cru Pinot Noir to one of Chardonnay, with jasmine, pear and clementine.

guests.a: Barbe-Nicole Clicquot Ponsardin, widowed in 1805 at twenty seven, who took over her husband's family business and led it for decades. The house credits her with the riddling table and the first known blended rosé.

guests.q: Is La Grande Dame a fancier Yellow Label?
guests.a: No. Yellow Label is the non vintage blend of the three grapes from many crus; La Grande Dame is a vintage wine from eight Grand Cru villages, about nine tenths Pinot Noir.

guests.q: Is it the same as Bollinger's La Grande Année?
guests.a: No, the names only sound alike. La Grande Dame is Veuve Clicquot's, of Reims, named for the widow; La Grande Année is Bollinger's vintage wine, of Aÿ.
No, it is a Brut: the house gave the 2015 6 grams of sugar a litre, drier than Yellow Label.

traps: The riddling table is credited to the widow Clicquot, not to Dom Perignon.
La Grande Dame is Pinot Noir dominant, not a blanc de blancs.
La Grande Dame is Veuve Clicquot's; La Grande Année is Bollinger's and Grand Siècle is Laurent-Perrier's.
La Grande Dame's first vintage is 1962 and its launch 1972, the house's bicentenary: two different years for one wine.

sheet.label: La Grande Dame
sheet.note: The sheet and the label agree. The wine is always a vintage, so the label also carries its year, and the rosé of the same name is a separate wine.

cards.front: Veuve Clicquot: name its prestige cuvée on the class sheet, and the grape that leads it.
cards.back: La Grande Dame, the vintage wine: Pinot Noir led, about nine tenths since the 2008 vintage, with Chardonnay for the rest.

cards.front: La Grande Dame: which house makes it, and for whom is it named?
cards.back: Veuve Clicquot, of Reims, named for Barbe-Nicole Clicquot Ponsardin, the widow who took over the house in 1805.

cards.front: La Grande Dame: its first vintage, and the year and occasion of its launch?
cards.back: The 1962, launched in 1972 for the house's bicentenary.

questions.q: Which prestige cuvée is named for the widow who took over her late husband's family business at Reims in 1805?
questions.exp: La Grande Dame is Veuve Clicquot's, named for Barbe-Nicole Clicquot Ponsardin. La Grande Année is Bollinger's, Grand Siècle is Laurent-Perrier's, and Femme de Champagne, the other cuvée named for a woman, is Duval-Leroy's.

questions.q: What does Veuve Clicquot credit its widow with inventing in 1816?
opts: The wire cage over the cork
questions.exp: The house credits Barbe-Nicole Clicquot with the riddling table of 1816, the ancestor of the rack, made to clear the wine of its sediment. The clear flat bottomed bottle is Louis Roederer's, made for Cristal.

questions.q: Since the 2008 vintage, by the house, about how much of La Grande Dame is Pinot Noir?
opts: None, it is a Blanc de Blancs
questions.exp: From the 2008 the house raised Pinot Noir to about nine tenths, with Chardonnay for the rest; earlier vintages held between half and two thirds. It has never been a Blanc de Blancs.

report: Built on the library's p-veuve-clicquot, contradicting it nowhere; its two traps are kept word for word, Dom Perignon spelt as the library prints it.

Barbe-Nicole Clicquot Ponsardin's dates: 1777 by the house, 1866 by Wikipedia and Decanter. Her father-in-law and her partner are described, not named, their dates not sought; the partner's official headship from 1841 is Wikipedia's and Decanter's, and the refuter cut his family's keeping of the house until the 1980s, which rested on one book as a search summary gave it.
The riddling table of 1816 and the blended rosé of 1818 are the house's claims and told as such; the plan's first known blended rosé matches the house's own words.
The first vintage: the 1962 was launched in 1972 by two accounts, but one says the first wide release was the 1966 and a merchant says the 1969, so first.what says accounts differ.

Ownership: Louis Vuitton's purchase of 1986 and the group of 1987 are Wikipedia's; the Oxford Companion dates the joining to 1987. Henriot's trade of its house for a share in Veuve Clicquot, told undated in Henriot's record, is left out here.
kind.code: the letters NM were not read on a label; they are inferred from the house buying from fifty to sixty crus.

The blend in words: the house gives 61 per cent Pinot Noir for the 2004, 53 for the 2006, 92 for the 2008 and 90 for the 2012 and 2015, so the record says half to two thirds before the 2008 and about nine tenths since.
The eight Grand Cru villages are named on the house's page of the 1990; the 2012 drew its Chardonnay from Avize and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger alone, so the villages move by vintage.
Time on lees: no house figure was found; the disgorging of October 2021 rests on one merchant's sheet and is told as that.
The Yellow Label figures move between the house's pages (reserve 25 to 50, 30 to 45 or up to 45 per cent; dosage 9 or 10 grams; 30 months or three years), so the record gives the most repeated.
La Grande Dame Rosé's first vintage was not found and is left out; Clos Colin's date of purchase, 1741 by the house, is left out as it falls before the founding year and was not explained.
cuvee.bottle is empty: the bottle's later designs were not sourced, and the artist who dressed one is living.

changed: story: the partner's family keeping the house until 1986 cut (one book); Louis Vuitton's purchase of 1986 kept.
story: the widow's vineyards known for Pinot Noir cut, no source carrying it.
style.dosage, guests[3].a: Yellow Label at 9 to 10 grams, by the house's pages and Wine Spectator.
cuvee.lees: two disgorgings of the 2015, October 2021 and July 2023.
cuvee.rhythm: the vintages named without saying what the house's pages show.
open: NM was not read on a label: no listing with the code was found; the letters rest on the house buying from fifty to sixty crus.

Malolactic stopped in some wineries since 2018 rests on the house's own page as the author read it; an older Wine Spectator article has every wine through malolactic, so a refuter's second source was not found.
Which vintage of La Grande Dame was first sold widely (1962, 1966 or 1969) stays unsettled, as first.what says.
Yellow Label's reserve share moves by source (26 to 45 per cent).
